entry: Head of the [[Catholic Church]] and ruler of the [[Papal States]], 1073–85. Born Hildebrand in Sovana, in southern Tuscany, he served earlier popes as a monk and administrator before his election. He was a leading figure in the Gregorian Reform, which targeted simony and clerical marriage and asserted papal independence from secular rulers. He was the first pope to impose obligatory [[Celibacy|celibacy]] on the clergy, which had until then commonly married. His central dispute was the [[Investiture Controversy]] with Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV over papal authority and the right to appoint bishops. Gregory excommunicated Henry three times, and Henry appointed the antipope Clement III in opposition. The Dictatus Papae of 1075 set out 27 papal claims, including the sole power to depose bishops. Denounced during his reign for the autocratic use of papal power, Gregory was later hailed as one of the greatest of the Roman pontiffs.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] and sovereign of the [[Papal States]], 1198–1216. Elected at age 37, Innocent III was one of the most powerful medieval popes, claiming supremacy over Europe's kings. His decretals and the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 advanced church reform and considerably refined Western canon law. He used interdicts and other censures to compel princes to obey him, with mixed success. He greatly extended the [[Crusades]], directing campaigns against Muslim Iberia, the Holy Land and the pagans of Livonia, and the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars of southern France. The Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) ended in the sack of Constantinople, which went against his explicit orders. He reluctantly accepted the outcome as God's will to reunite the Latin and [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox]] churches, though the sack deepened hostility between them.

Polish-born head of the [[Catholic Church]] and sovereign of [[Vatican City]], 1978–2005. Karol Józef Wojtyła was the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI in the 16th century. Before his election he had been archbishop of Kraków and a cardinal. He pursued ecumenism with Judaism, [[Islam]] and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]], and named atheism the greatest threat. He kept the Church's positions on abortion, artificial contraception, the ordination of women and clerical celibacy, and read the reforms of the [[Second Vatican Council]] in a generally conventional way. He visited 129 countries, beatified 1,344 people and canonized 483 saints, more than the combined tally of his predecessors in the preceding five centuries. He has been credited with helping to end communist rule in Poland and elsewhere in Europe, and criticized for not acting more firmly against the sexual abuse of children by priests.

Italian-born head of the [[Catholic Church]] and sovereign of [[Vatican City]], 1958–63. Elected at age 76 after the death of Pius XII, he was expected to be a caretaker pope, but he called the [[Second Vatican Council]] (1962–65), which opened the Church to change and to dialogue with other churches. He stressed the Church's pastoral role and ended the practice of formulating policy automatically from old theological propositions. In Italy he barred bishops from interfering in local elections. His Ostpolitik sought dialogue with communist Eastern Europe, and he reached out to the [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox]] churches. He enlarged the College of Cardinals to 85, dropping the traditional limit of 70, and named the first cardinals from Africa, Japan and the Philippines. He was beatified in 2000 by [[Pope John Paul II]] and canonized in 2014 by Pope Francis, and is affectionately known as "the Good Pope."

Head of the [[Catholic Church]] and ruler of the [[Papal States]], 1503–13. Nicknamed the Warrior Pope, he personally led papal forces, including at the Siege of Mirandola, during the [[Italian Wars]]. He centralized the Papal States, joined the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508, and formed the Holy League against France in 1511, which forced French troops back behind the Alps. As a patron of the High Renaissance, he established the [[Vatican Museums]] in 1506 and began rebuilding [[St. Peter's Basilica]]. He commissioned the [[Raphael]] Rooms and [[Michelangelo]]'s paintings in the [[Sistine Chapel]], and he allowed people seeking indulgences to donate money for the basilica. Erasmus of Rotterdam satirized him after his death in *Julius Excluded from Heaven*.

Roman aristocrat and bishop of [[Rome]], 440–61, known as Leo the Great. He developed ideas of papal authority based on the apostolic succession from [[Saint Peter]]. In 452 he met [[Attila|Attila the Hun]] and persuaded him to turn back from Italy, though historians debate how much his personal authority contributed. The Council of Chalcedon (451) acclaimed his Tome, a letter explaining how the divine and human natures of Christ were united in one person. Benedict XIV named him a Doctor of the Church. He suppressed Manichaeism in Rome and opposed Priscillianism in [[Spain]]. During his papacy the word *pope*, which had meant any bishop, came to mean only the bishop of Rome.

Head of the [[Catholic Church]], 1846–78, whose reign of nearly 32 years is the longest verified papal reign. He began as a liberal reformer who eased restrictions on Jewish movement and granted an amnesty to revolutionaries. After the Revolutions of 1848, when his prime minister was assassinated and he fled Rome, his approach changed radically. He excommunicated participants in the Roman Republic and grew increasingly conservative. He was behind the Mortara case (1858), in which a six-year-old Jewish boy was taken from his family by force. His 1864 Syllabus of Errors condemned liberalism, secularization and the separation of church and state. He convened the First Vatican Council, which defined papal infallibility in 1870 before breaking off and never reconvening. When the [[Kingdom of Italy]] captured Rome that year, he declared himself a "prisoner in the Vatican" and refused to leave [[Vatican City]]. [[Pope John Paul II]] beatified him in 2000.

French-born head of the [[Catholic Church]] and ruler of the [[Papal States]], 1088–99. Before his election he had been prior of Cluny and cardinal-bishop of Ostia. He supported the Gregorian reforms against simony, lay investiture and clerical marriage, and he faced the antipope Clement III, who held Rome. He is best known for the Council of Clermont (1095), where he called for an armed pilgrimage to recover the Holy Land from Muslims and promised forgiveness of sins to those who went. This began the [[First Crusade]] (1096–99), which captured Jerusalem in 1097. Urban died before news of the capture reached him. He also established the modern Roman Curia on the model of a royal ecclesiastical court, and he supported the work of [[Anselm of Canterbury]].

Cartoon sailor created by Elzie Crisler Segar. Popeye the Sailor Man first appeared on January 17, 1929, in the daily comic strip *Thimble Theater*, where he quickly became the lead character. In 1933 Max Fleischer adapted him into theatrical cartoon shorts for [[Paramount Pictures]], which were among the most popular of the 1930s. Popeye gains superhuman strength from [[Spinach|spinach]] and fights the bully Bluto for Olive Oyl. He has also appeared in [[Comic book|comic books]], television cartoons and advertising, and the 1980 live-action film starred [[Robin Williams]].

Sacred narrative of the K'iche' [[Maya peoples|Maya]] of highland [[Guatemala]]. It recounts the Maya [[Creation myth|creation myth]], the exploits of the Hero Twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué, and the history of the K'iche' people. Its name is translated as "Book of the Community" or "Book of Counsel." The text was preserved orally until about 1550, when it was recorded in writing. In the 18th century the Dominican friar Francisco Ximénez transcribed it in K'iche' with a parallel Spanish translation. The manuscript is now in the Newberry Library in [[Chicago]]. Because missionaries and colonists destroyed many documents after the Spanish conquest, the text is among the few sources on Mesoamerican mythology.

Increase in the median age of a population, usually reflected in rising mean and median ages, a falling share of children and a rising share of older people. Two forces drive it: longer [[Longevity|longevity]] and declining [[Fertility|fertility]], although falling fertility now accounts for most of the aging. Aging began in most developed countries in the late 19th century, and by the late 20th century the world population as a whole was aging. The number of people aged 60 and over has tripled since 1950, reaching 600 million in 2000 and passing 700 million in 2006. The combined senior and geriatric population is projected to reach 2.1 billion by 2050. The [[United Nations]] expects aging to be faster in the 21st century than in the 20th. Policies include measures that increase the young working-age population and changes that adapt pensions and health care to older populations.

Group of individuals of the same [[Species|species]], separated from other groups by characteristics such as living area, genetic attributes or demographic structure. Definitions vary among biologists. The word derives from the [[Latin]] *populatio*, "a people, a multitude." Two main approaches define a population. The [[Ecology|ecological]] view treats its members as interacting and competing in a geographic area, while the evolutionary view treats genes and reproduction as the driving forces, and each population has its own gene pool. Some biologists define a population as individuals that can interbreed, and reproductive isolation separates populations and defines species. Terms such as deme, metapopulation and subpopulation describe other kinds of group. In ecology, the term community is generally used for several species of a region.

Sharp reduction in the size of a [[Population (biology)|population]]. Famines, earthquakes, floods, disease and droughts can cause one, as can human actions such as [[Genocide|genocide]] and intentional culling. The survivors carry less genetic diversity, which weakens the population's ability to adapt to environmental change. [[Genetic drift]] can then fix or eliminate alleles, and [[Inbreeding]] becomes more likely. Bottlenecks are central to conservation biology. North American [[American bison|bison]] fell from approximately 40 million to fewer than 1,000 by the early 1900s through overhunting.

headword: Population transfer in the Soviet Union
sort_key: population transfer in the soviet union
entry: Forced deportations and resettlements carried out by the Soviet government from 1930 to 1952, on the orders of [[Joseph Stalin]] and under the NKVD official [[Lavrentiy Beria]]. They included deportations of "anti-Soviet" groups, of entire ethnic groups, labor transfers and migrations to fill emptied territories. Dekulakization was the first deportation of an entire class, and the 1937 deportation of Soviet Koreans was the first of an entire nationality. Most destinations were remote areas of [[Siberia]] and [[Central Asia]]. At least 6 million people were affected. Historian Nicolas Werth places overall deaths at 1 to 1.5 million. The deportation of the [[Tatars|Crimean Tatars]] has been declared a genocide by Ukraine and other countries, and the [[European Parliament]] made the same declaration for the Chechens and Ingush. In 1991 the Russian republic's Supreme Soviet, under [[Boris Yeltsin]], denounced mass deportations as "Stalin's policy of defamation and genocide."

Contested concept for political stances that emphasize the "common people," often in opposition to a perceived elite. It is often associated with anti-establishment sentiment and has frequently carried a pejorative tone since the late 19th century. The word first appeared in English in 1858, as the antonym of "aristocratic." In the [[Russian Empire]] of the 1860s and 1870s, the term was associated with the narodniki, an agrarian movement, while in the United States the People's Party of the 1880s to early 1900s championed small farmers. In 1954 the sociologist Edward Shils used the term for anti-elite trends in U.S. society during the rise of [[McCarthyism]]. One later definition describes populism as a thin-centered ideology that divides society into a pure people and a corrupt elite, which can attach to left-wing or right-wing ideologies. Scholars disagree about its effects on liberal democracy.

Ceramic material made by heating raw materials, generally including [[Kaolinite]], in a kiln to between 1,200 and 1,400 °C. Its strength and translucence come mainly from vitrification and the formation of mullite within the body. It has usually been regarded as the most prestigious type of pottery, and it is used for [[Tableware|tableware]], figurines, electrical insulators and laboratory ware. The three main types are hard-paste, soft-paste and bone china. Porcelain originated in China, where the technology matured between approximately 200 and 800 CE, depending on the definition used. It spread to Asia and then Europe, and it was called "china" in English because it was first imported from China in the 17th century. The earliest European porcelain was made at the Meissen factory in [[Saxony]] in the early 18th century. In 2021 the global market for porcelain tableware was estimated at US$22.1 billion.

Large [[Rodent|rodent]] with a coat of sharp spines, or quills, that protect it from predators. The name comes from the [[Latin]] *porcus* ("pig") and *spina* ("spine"). Porcupines belong to two families that are not closely related. Old World porcupines (Hystricidae) live in Italy, West and South Asia and most of Africa; they are large, terrestrial and strictly nocturnal. New World porcupines (Erethizontidae) are native to North America and northern [[South America]], and they live in wooded areas and can climb trees. The largest species is the third-largest living rodent, after the [[Capybara|capybara]] and the [[Beaver|beaver]]. Quills are modified hairs made of keratin, and their display advertises that the animal is unsuitable as prey. Most porcupines are about 60–90 cm long. A baby porcupine, or porcupette, has soft quills that harden within days.

Mexican army general and politician, leader of Mexico, 1876–1911. Born in Oaxaca, he studied law, and [[Benito Juárez]] was among his mentors. He fought in the Reform War and against the French, and in June 1867 he led the forces that retook Mexico City. He then revolted against Juárez and Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada over the principle of no reelection, and he seized power in 1876. In 1884 he abandoned that principle and held office continuously until 1911. His regime ended political instability and brought economic growth. Its technocrats, known as científicos, benefited allies and foreign investors, while large estates grew through violence and legal abuse, provoking repression, strikes and uprisings. The period, the Porfiriato, has been called a de facto [[Dictatorship|dictatorship]]. In 1910 Díaz, then 80, ran for an eighth term despite a 1908 statement favoring democracy. Francisco I. Madero's opposition led to the [[Mexican Revolution]], and in May 1911 Díaz resigned and went into exile in [[Paris]].

Culinary name for the meat of the [[Pig|pig]]. Pork is eaten both fresh and preserved, as in ham, gammon, bacon and [[Sausage|sausage]]. Charcuterie is the branch of cooking devoted to prepared meats, many of them pork. Pigs were among the earliest domesticated animals, in Mesopotamia and China. Pork accounts for about 34% of meat production worldwide. It is popular in Central Europe and across the Western world, and Chinese cuisine esteems it highly; [[China]] is the world's largest pork consumer. Feijoada, the national dish of [[Brazil]], is traditionally made with pork trimmings. Some religions and cultures prohibit pork, notably Islam and Judaism.

Canadian-owned video-sharing website for [[Pornography|pornographic]] material, one of several sites owned by Aylo. It launched on May 25, 2007, and was bought in 2010 as part of the Manwin conglomerate, now Aylo. In 2020, after a *New York Times* exposé of non-consensual pornography and sex trafficking, Mastercard and Visa stopped processing payments to the site. Pornhub then removed videos from unverified users, cutting its content from 13 million to 4 million videos. In September 2025 Aylo agreed to pay $5 million to settle U.S. Federal Trade Commission and [[Utah]] charges of deceiving users about safeguards against child exploitation.

Performer in [[Pornographic film|pornographic films]], which present sexual fantasies. Performers are chosen mainly for their ability to fit a fantasy or genre, such as straight, gay or interracial scenes. The United States industry was the first to develop a star system; elsewhere the star system is uncommon and most actors are amateurs. Most performers use pseudonyms and seek anonymity. Few cross over into mainstream film, although some, such as [[Jenna Jameson]], have built businesses like ClubJenna. In 2011 roughly 1,200–1,500 performers were working in California's "Porn Valley."

Film presenting sexually explicit subject matter to arouse or satisfy the viewer. Films are classed as [[Softcore pornography|softcore]], showing nudity in suggestive situations, or [[Hardcore pornography|hardcore]], depicting penetration or extreme fetish acts. The first erotic film, the seven-minute *Le Coucher de la Mariée* (1896), showed a bathroom striptease. Viewing was often private, at [[Brothel|brothels]] or adult theaters. In the 1970s the Golden Age of Porn semi-legitimized the genre, and *Deep Throat* reached mainstream theatrical release. From the late 1990s the Internet changed distribution and complicated [[Censorship|censorship]].

Sexually suggestive material, such as pictures, videos, text or audio, intended for [[Sexual arousal|sexual arousal]]. Depictions date to the [[Upper Paleolithic]], and the oldest artifacts considered pornographic, found in Germany, are at least 35,000 years old. Reception has varied by culture. The [[Kama Sutra]] was celebrated, while the English novel *Fanny Hill* (1748) became one of the most prosecuted books. In 1969 *Blue Movie*, by [[Andy Warhol]], became the first film to depict unsimulated sex with a wide U.S. theatrical release, and the "Golden Age of Porn" followed (1969–1984). Home video and the [[World Wide Web|web]] led to global growth, and 2023 estimates put the total market value at over US$172 billion. Research on its effects is contested. Meta-analyses find small-to-moderate associations with anxiety, depression and relationship dissatisfaction, especially for problematic use, but causality is unestablished. Feminist groups are divided, with some seeking to abolish it and others opposing censorship.

Small, dolphin-like [[Cetacean|cetacean]] of the family Phocoenidae. Porpoises have flattened, spade-shaped teeth and lack the pronounced beak of most [[Dolphin|dolphins]], and they are more closely related to [[Narwhal|narwhals]] and belugas. They range from the [[Vaquita|vaquita]], about 1.4 m long, to Dall's porpoise, about 2.3 m and 220 kg. They use echolocation as their primary sense and feed mainly on fish and squid. Porpoises live in habitats from rivers to the open ocean. Bycatch in gill nets is a major threat, and the vaquita is nearly extinct, with a predicted population of fewer than a dozen individuals. Since the extinction of the baiji, it has been considered the most endangered cetacean.

Semi-solid food made by soaking, poaching or boiling starchy plants, typically grain, in milk or water. It is a traditional staple in many countries and is often flavored with salt, sugar, honey or fruit, or made savory with spices, meat or vegetables. In British English the word refers specifically to oat porridge, known as [[Oat|oatmeal]] in North America. Other variants include polenta, made from [[Maize|maize]]; poi, made from [[Taro|taro]]; congee, an Asian savory rice porridge; and gruel, a thinner form of oat porridge. Porridge originated over 12,000 years ago, after the domestication of grains. A 2014 review found that at least 3 grams of oat beta-glucan daily lowered total and low-density lipoprotein [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]] by 5–10%. In Charles Dickens's *Oliver Twist*, gruel marks poverty.
